cues.text: MIT 8113, Digital Transformation and Innovation.
This is Study Session 3, titled Change Management and Customer Experience Design.
We begin with the first chapter, change management fundamentals.
Start with a question.
Suppose an organisation buys excellent new software, installs it correctly, and switches it on.
Is the transformation finished?
This chapter says no, and the reason sits at the heart of digital transformation.
Here is the definition.
Change management is the structured process of helping individuals and organisations move from a current state to a desired future state.
Two things in that sentence matter.
First, it is structured, so it is planned and deliberate rather than left to chance.
Second, it covers both individuals and organisations.
The organisation moves, but only because the people inside it move.
The source lists what this process includes: communication, leadership, participation, readiness, training, feedback and reinforcement.
Take them one at a time.
Communication means people hear what is changing and why.
Leadership means someone visibly guides the move.
Participation means the people affected take part rather than simply receiving instructions.
Readiness means checking whether people and teams are actually prepared before the change arrives.
Training gives them the skills to work in the new way.
Feedback lets their experiences flow back to those leading the change.
Reinforcement keeps the new behaviour in place, so people do not slide back to old habits once the excitement fades.
Now the distinction this block draws.
Technical implementation changes systems.
Organisational change management changes how people actually work.
The first concerns software, hardware, data and configuration.
The second concerns daily behaviour, routines and decisions.
The source says the latter is essential to adoption and value realisation.
Adoption means people really use the new thing.
Value realisation means the organisation actually receives the benefits it expected.
So a system can be technically perfect and still deliver nothing if people do not change how they work.
As a simple analogy, and this is a teaching illustration rather than a source claim, think of a new road that is fully built but that nobody drives on because everyone still uses the old route.
The road exists, but its value is never realised.
Next, the trade-offs.
The source gives the advantages first: reduced uncertainty, better adoption, alignment, productivity and sustained results.
Reduced uncertainty means people know what to expect.
Better adoption means more people actually use the change.
Alignment means people and teams pull in the same direction.
Productivity and sustained results mean the benefits are not only reached but maintained over time.
Then the opposite side.
Poorly managed change causes disruption, stress, resistance, lost skills and customer dissatisfaction.
Disruption interrupts normal work.
Stress falls on the people living through the change.
Resistance is people pushing back against it.
Lost skills occurs when experienced people leave or when old expertise is no longer used.
Customer dissatisfaction follows when internal turmoil reaches the people the organisation serves.
The source adds an important qualification.
Formal change programmes also require time, money and leadership attention.
They are not free.
For that reason, the source warns you to avoid excessive bureaucracy.
The aim is a structured approach, not a heavy process of forms and approvals that slows everything down.
Good change management is proportionate to the change it supports.
The final block is about stakeholders.
Stakeholders include sponsors, managers, employees, customers, suppliers, regulators and partners.
A stakeholder is anyone who affects the change or is affected by it.
Notice how wide this list is.
It reaches beyond the organisation's own staff to customers, suppliers, regulators and partners.
The source tells you to map their influence, impact and concerns.
That gives three questions for each stakeholder group.
How much influence do they have over whether the change succeeds?
How much will the change impact them?
And what are they worried about?
Answering these helps you decide whom to involve, how to communicate with them, and where resistance may appear.
Now the roles.
A sponsor owns the vision and the resources.
So the sponsor is the person or group who says where the organisation is going and who provides the means to get there.
Change agents support local adoption.
They work close to the teams, helping colleagues start using the change in their own setting.
Managers translate goals into daily work.
They take the high-level vision and turn it into what people actually do from one day to the next.
Customers and employees provide feedback.
They are not only recipients of the change but a key source of information about whether it is working.
The source ends with a clear message: change is not only the responsibility of HR or IT.
Human resources and information technology each play a part, but responsibility is shared across sponsors, managers, change agents and the wider group of stakeholders.
If you leave change to a single department, you lose the leadership, the local support and the feedback that make it succeed.
To pull the chapter together: change management moves people and organisations from a current state to a desired future state.
It differs from technical implementation because it changes how people work, and that is what delivers adoption and value.
It brings real benefits but also real costs, so it should be structured without being bureaucratic.
And it depends on many stakeholders, each with a role to play.
